source.title_on_document: LLM Randomness and Creativity: An Experiment on Human-AI Collaboration

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplement, online appendix, preregistration, data, or code.
supplement.holds: Nothing referenced. No SDs of the performance outcomes (semantic distance, RAT accuracy) are printed. The only arm-level means of these outcomes are in the Discussion: RAT accuracy of 45 percent without AI against 55 percent with AI (the two AI cells pooled), and AI-user subsample figures. Table I holds only survey constructs and cell counts. The DAT regressions are not reported.

paper_design_summary: In December 2025, Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of nine cells of a 3 x 3 between-subjects design: no AI, an LLM chat assistant at temperature 0.1 (low randomness), or the same assistant at temperature 1.2 (high randomness), crossed with one of three tasks (Remote Associates Test, Alternate Uses Task, Divergent Association Task), each done for three rounds. Of the 775 people analyzed after exclusions, 519 had the assistant available, its use was optional, and 251 of them used it. RAT responses were scored by accuracy, and AUT and DAT responses by the mean and maximum pairwise semantic distance (spaCy embeddings) among each participant's own responses.

participants.exclusions: 960 participants were recruited on Prolific, separate from a 40-person pilot. Those who did not complete the study or failed an attention check were excluded, leaving 775 analyzed. Randomization happened mid-survey, after the verbal fluency task. The paper does not say how many of the 185 excluded had been assigned, so no count at assignment is given and the analysis is not called intention-to-treat. The analyzed cell counts in Table I sum to 775 (AUT 213, DAT 245, RAT 317). Within each task the three cells are near equal, but the task totals differ, and the paper gives neither the task allocation ratio nor exclusions by cell.

ai_tool.name_model: not stated: an unnamed LLM assistant with temperature 0.1 (low randomness) or 1.2 (high randomness); the paper names no model or provider
ai_tool.how_used: A chat panel beside the task on a custom platform (Figure 1: 'I'm here to help if you need suggestions or want to brainstorm ideas. Just type your question below.'). Use was optional. The paper prints that 48.7 percent (251 of 519) of the analyzed participants with access used it. Non-use among them: AUT 58 of 145, RAT 118 of 212, DAT 92 of 162. Telemetry logged the interactions and the share of AI-generated words incorporated into responses.

task.description: Each participant did one task for three rounds: the Remote Associates Test (find the fourth word that links three cue words; convergent thinking), the Alternate Uses Task (creative uses of a common object such as a paperclip, at least 3 ideas per round per Figure 1), or the Divergent Association Task (list ten words as unrelated to each other as possible). A one-minute verbal fluency task came before randomization.
task.duration: Three rounds; total time not stated (time on task is a regression control).

outcomes.name: AUT average semantic distance among a participant's own responses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Semantic-distance score of a divergent-thinking test: spaCy en_core_web_md 300-dimensional embeddings of each response, then the mean of all pairwise cosine distances (1 - similarity) within one participant's set of responses. Each participant did three rounds (at least 3 ideas per round per Figure 1), and the paper does not say whether the set pools all three rounds or each round is scored separately. The paper calls it creative performance measured as semantic diversity and names mean and maximum distance its 'two primary metrics'. Coded flexibility because it measures variety among one person's own ideas, not across people. Coded automated_score because the paper uses it as the creativity score of the test. Regression on condition dummies, with Low randomness as the omitted condition, controlling for duration_seconds and AI_used. The estimator, regression N, and standard-error type are not stated.

Sign reversed: the coefficient is NoAI relative to Low randomness. The regression controls for AI_used, a post-assignment variable. Regression N not printed.

outcomes.name: DAT mean semantic distance among the words a participant generated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The AUT procedure of S1-O1 applied to the DAT words: the mean pairwise spaCy cosine distance 'between all generated words', computed 'using the identical computational procedure'. Each DAT round asks for 10 words ('Participants generated 10 semantically different words'), and each participant did three rounds. The paper does not say whether a score covers one round's 10 words or the words of all three rounds. The maximum distance, merged with this outcome in the reconciled form, is now S1-O5. Coded flexibility and automated_score for the reasons given in S1-O1. Section IV says each outcome was regressed on condition, controlling for time on task and AI use, and that no DAT coefficient was significant, so none is reported.

company_involvement.description: None stated. The authors are at the University of Arizona, the paper has no funding statement, and it names no model or provider.

eligibility.reason: Individuals on Prolific were randomly assigned to one of nine cells: no AI or an LLM assistant at temperature 0.1 or 1.2, crossed with task (PDF p. 2, Section III.B). The analysis keeps 775 people after exclusions (PDF p. 3). Each task's analyzed subsample exceeds 50 (AUT 213, DAT 245, RAT 317), and the smallest analyzed cell has 68 (Table I, PDF p. 4). Outcomes are computed on participants' responses: semantic distance for the AUT and DAT, accuracy for the RAT (PDF pp. 2-3). Caveats: AI use was optional (251 of the 519 analyzed participants with access used it), the regressions control for post-assignment AI use, the RAT outcome is convergent (a codebook open question), and the AUT and DAT measures are within-person variety rather than rated creativity. The final-pass corrections (the DAT mean and maximum split into S1-O3 and S1-O5, the DAT word pool no longer stated, two AI-user contrasts added) change no criterion.

one_line_finding: Neither LLM temperature nor AI availability changed AUT semantic distance (HighRandomness -0.008, SE 0.037; NoAI -0.002, SE 0.044; Table II, PDF p. 4) or DAT scores (not significant and not reported, PDF p. 3), and Table III shows no significant condition coefficient for RAT accuracy after controlling for AI use (HighRandomness -0.074, SE 0.049; NoAI -0.044, SE 0.055; PDF p. 5), though the Discussion reports that AI availability raised RAT accuracy from 45 to 55 percent (p < .05, PDF p. 3).
open_questions: The Table II and III regressions control for AI_used, a post-assignment, self-selected variable, so the NoAI and HighRandomness coefficients are not intention-to-treat contrasts. The only unadjusted AI-versus-no-AI comparison is the RAT 45 versus 55 percent in the Discussion, printed with p < .05 only. No other arm means and no SDs of the performance outcomes are printed.
The regression N, the regression unit (participant or participant-round), the estimator, and the standard-error type are not printed.

Whether each AUT and DAT semantic-distance score pools a participant's three rounds or is computed per round. The paper says only 'each participant's set of responses' and 'all generated words', and the DAT asks for 10 words per round.
The paper does not say how many of the 185 exclusions (non-completers and attention-check failures) happened after randomization, so no count at assignment is available.

Task totals are unequal (AUT 213, DAT 245, RAT 317), while the three cells within each task are near equal. The paper gives no task allocation ratio and no exclusions by cell, so task-specific dropout cannot be ruled out. Every AI contrast compares cells within one task.

Whether the AUT and DAT within-participant semantic distance should be coded flexibility (codebook: variety among one person's own ideas) or overall_creativity (the paper calls it creative performance).
Whether RAT accuracy (convergent) belongs beside rated creativity (codebook open question).

Measure code for RAT accuracy (S1-O4): no codebook measure code fits answer-key accuracy, so automated_score is a placeholder until Review 1 adds a code or a convention (the same gap as in final c082).
The paper says p-values for 'this and all following results' are Holm-adjusted (PDF p. 3), but the Table II and III notes give plain thresholds. Whether the table stars are adjusted is unclear.

The AI-user subsample comparisons (AUT average distance 0.51 vs 0.31, with maximum distance described only as 'consistent'; RAT 64 percent among users against 45 percent without AI; RAT 72 vs 57 percent) condition on post-assignment AI use and print no SE, SD, or n.

notes: Single 6-page proceedings paper. Tables I to III and Figure 1 were read on the PDF page images. The markdown conversion renders the Discussion's '0.1-1.2 range' as '0.11.2 range'; quotes follow the PDF (p. 3). Task names vary: 'Remote Associates Test' in the abstract but 'Random Associates Task (RAT)' in Section III.A, and 'Alternate Uses Test' in the abstract but 'Alternate Uses Task (AUT)' in Section III.A. For the AUT the paper also reports a correlation between the share of AI-generated words incorporated and semantic distance (r = -.399, p < .001; PDF p. 3). It is a post-assignment association, not a contrast between assigned conditions, so it is not recorded as a contrast (screener B had listed it). The Discussion adds that high reliance on the AI went with lower average and maximum semantic distance for the AUT but not the DAT (PDF p. 4). Self-reported outcomes (process and outcome satisfaction, perceived effort, ownership, intrinsic motivation, and self-rated creativity before and after the task) are not listed because they are not scored on the output. Table I gives their cell means. For the RAT, outcome satisfaction was lower without AI than with Low (p < .01) and High randomness (p < .001), Holm-adjusted, and perceived effort was higher without AI (p < .01) for the RAT only (PDF p. 3). AI use: the paper prints 48.7 percent (251 of 519), but the counts give 48.4 percent. Non-use was AUT 58 of 145, RAT 118 of 212, DAT 92 of 162, chi2(2, 519) = 10.96, p = .004. AI used as first resort: AUT 48 of 145, RAT 27 of 212, DAT 14 of 162 (PDF p. 3). A one-minute verbal fluency task came before randomization and is not an outcome. The paper cites Kumar et al. (2025) as related work but analyzes its own new sample. Final pass (2026-10-05): the three challenge files were checked against the PDF pages and the markdown. The assignment and people lenses found no problems. Of the five outcome-lens problems, four were corrected: the DAT mean and maximum distances are now separate outcomes (S1-O3 and the new S1-O5, so S1-O4 keeps its id), the DAT outcomes no longer state a 10-word pool, and S1-O2 and S1-O4 each gained an AI-user contrast (maximum distance High vs Low; RAT AI users vs no AI). The fifth, the automated_score code for RAT accuracy, stays open as a labeled placeholder, as in final c082. Spec alignment and accuracy edits: counts after exclusions now say 'analyzed' (paper_design_summary, participants.exclusions, ai_tool.how_used, eligibility.reason); source.supplement.holds and the first open question no longer say that no arm means are printed, because the Discussion gives the no-AI RAT accuracy of 45 percent; one_line_finding now says 'condition coefficient', because AI_used is significant in Table III; the AUT outcomes note that the paper does not say whether a score pools the three rounds. The reconciliation object is unchanged.

differences.resolved: automated_score (A). The paper uses the embedding distance as the creative-performance score of two divergent-thinking tests, which matches the codebook's automated_score ('semantic-distance scoring of divergent-thinking tests'). Reconciled c054 used the same rule and chose embedding_similarity only because that paper did not present its distance as a creativity score. measure_detail records the embedding basis.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O4 (RAT accuracy) is coded automated_score, which codebook Section 6 defines as a scoring model for creativity, while the paper divides correct answers by problems attempted and uses no scoring model. The form's own measure_detail said no code fits.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: The checker is right that automated_score does not fit, but no codebook measure code fits answer-key accuracy and the spec's measure list has no 'other'. The source settles what the measure is; only a codebook decision can settle the code. measure stays automated_score as a labeled placeholder, as in final c082. S1-O4 measure_detail now says so, adds that the paper does not say how a response was judged correct, and drops 'scored against the answer key'. A new open question asks Review 1 for a code or a convention.
challenge_resolution.quote: The accuracy score was calculated as the number of correct responses divided by the total number of problems attempted.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 2 (printed p. 1771), Section III.C Measures, first paragraph (right column); codebook Section 6 (Measure)

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O3 merges the two DAT metrics (mean and maximum pairwise distance) into one outcome, while the AUT's two metrics are separate outcomes (S1-O1, S1-O2). Rule 7 merges only robustness variants, and an estimate is defined on one outcome.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: S1-O3 is now DAT mean semantic distance only. A new outcome S1-O5 holds DAT maximum distance, with the same two contrasts (DAT_High vs DAT_Low, ai_design; DAT_Low vs DAT_NoAI, ai_vs_bau; both no_clear_difference, statistics none). The new id lets RAT accuracy keep S1-O4. The sentence 'Treated as one outcome because neither is reported' is gone.
challenge_resolution.quote: we calculated the mean and maximum pairwise semantic distances between all generated words using the identical computational procedure.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 1772), Section III.C Measures, DAT paragraph (top of the left column); PDF p. 2 (printed p. 1771), Section III.C ('We computed two primary metrics.')

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O3's name and measure_detail say the distance is computed among a participant's 10 words, but each participant did three rounds and the paper does not state the pool.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: The S1-O3 and S1-O5 names now say 'among the words a participant generated'. Their measure_detail says each DAT round asks for 10 words, each participant did three rounds, and the paper does not say whether a score covers one round or all three. S1-O1 and S1-O2 measure_detail carry the same caveat for the AUT's 'set of responses', and a new open question records the pooling gap.
challenge_resolution.quote: In the experiment, participants are asked to complete one of these tasks for three rounds.
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 2 (printed p. 1771), Section III.A Design, end of the first paragraph, and Section III.B ('They complete 3 rounds of the task'); PDF p. 3 (printed p. 1772), Section III.C, DAT paragraph ('Participants generated 10 semantically different words')

challenge_resolution.problem: The RAT result for AI users (64 percent, p < .001), a comparison with the no-AI arm, sits in the 'reported' text of the pooled AI-available contrast instead of in a contrast of its own, unlike the form's other AI-user comparisons.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: S1-O4 gained the contrast 'RAT_High and RAT_Low pooled, participants who used the AI only' vs RAT_NoAI (ai_vs_bau, treatment_higher, p_value_only). Its reported text says the sentence names no comparison group, that 'the effect' is the rise from 45 percent without AI in the sentence before, that no SE, SD, or n is printed, and that the subsample is selected on post-assignment AI use. The 64 percent left the pooled contrast's reported text.
challenge_resolution.quote: The effect is even stronger if we look at the subsample of participants who actually used the AI assistant when available (accuracy was 64%, p < .001).
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 1772), Section V Discussion, second paragraph (right column)

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O2 (AUT maximum distance) has no AI-user High vs Low contrast, although the paper says the AI-user result is consistent for maximum distance and the parallel S1-O1 result is coded as its own contrast.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: S1-O2 gained the contrast 'AUT_High, participants who used the AI only' vs 'AUT_Low, participants who used the AI only' (ai_design, treatment_higher, statistics none). Its reported text says no number is printed for maximum distance. The sentence about AI users left the reported text of the full-sample HighRandomness contrast, whose locator is now Table II only.
challenge_resolution.quote: While this difference is only marginally significant, it is in the hypothesized direction (consistent results are found for maximum semantic distance).
challenge_resolution.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 1773), Section V Discussion, third paragraph (top of the left column)

open_items.item: The Table II and III regressions control for AI_used, a post-assignment variable, so their condition coefficients are not intention-to-treat contrasts, and no SDs and almost no arm means of the performance outcomes are printed. This matters for effect sizes and standard errors, not for eligibility, which rests on the assignment, the analyzed count, and how outputs were scored.
Regression N, unit (participant or participant-round), estimator, and standard-error type are not printed. This matters for codebook Section 10 (standard errors), not for eligibility.

Whether each AUT and DAT semantic-distance score pools a participant's three rounds or is computed per round (the DAT asks for 10 words per round). The score is computed on the participant's output under either reading, so criterion 3 holds.
How many of the 185 exclusions happened after randomization, so no count at assignment exists. Criterion 2 counts people analyzed, and 775 is far above 50.

Unequal task totals (AUT 213, DAT 245, RAT 317) against near-equal cells within each task, with no allocation ratio or exclusions by cell. Every AI contrast compares cells within one task, so random assignment of AI (criterion 1) is not in question.

Construct of the AUT and DAT within-participant semantic distance: flexibility (codebook rule for variety among one person's own ideas) or overall_creativity (the paper's 'creative performance'). Either construct is scored on the output.
Whether RAT accuracy (convergent) belongs beside rated creativity is a Review 1 decision (codebook Section 13). Eligibility rests on the AUT and DAT outcomes in any case.
Measure code for RAT accuracy (S1-O4): automated_score is a placeholder until Review 1 adds a code or a convention for answer-key accuracy, as in final c082.
Whether the Table II and III significance stars are Holm-adjusted, as the Section IV statement about 'this and all following results' suggests, or plain, as the table notes suggest.

The AI-user subsample comparisons (AUT 0.51 vs 0.31 and the 'consistent' maximum-distance result; RAT 64 percent against 45 percent without AI; RAT 72 vs 57 percent) condition on post-assignment AI use and print no SE, SD, or n. They are secondary to the assigned-arm contrasts.
